deck.brief: One worked page for each page-type form that examples/page-types.pages.json does not draw, on the same fictional regional rail operator, Northvale Rail. Each page stands alone - it compiles, composes and passes the page gates as the only page of a deck - and is printed by `author-deck.mjs --example <type>/<form>`. The file is a catalogue, not a deck to build. Every number is illustrative.
deck.question: Can Northvale Rail grow from 48 million to 60 million journeys a year by FY31, and how?

pages.title: Off-peak journeys passed their FY20 level in FY25 and kept growing

annotations.text: First year above the FY20 level of 16.1m

pages.bar: Off-peak demand is already growing on an hourly timetable, so the half-hourly service adds to a rising base rather than reviving a falling one.
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; ticket sales by time of travel

pages.title: Weekend journeys doubled from FY22 and now exceed their pre-pandemic level

annotations.text: 2.4m in the pandemic year, a third of FY20
Leisure travel returned first, a year before commuting did
9.9m, a fifth above FY20, on the same Saturday timetable

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: Season tickets never came back; day tickets carry the recovery
pages.rail: Season tickets carried 21.5 million journeys in FY20 and 12.4 million in FY26. Day and advance tickets filled the gap, so the revenue now depends on trips people choose week by week, which a better off-peak timetable can win and a poor one can lose.

annotations.text: Day returns are now 47% of journeys

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; ticket sales by product

pages.title: Punctuality slipped three points as train-km returned to its peak

points.lead: The network fills before it fails
points.text: Punctuality fell three points while train-km rose from 15.4 million to 18.2 million, because the added trains share the same two-track approach into Leeds. Each late train now delays the one behind it, which did not happen when the timetable had gaps.

The Eastern line runs at 86.1%, the weakest on the network, and its diesel units account for half of all fleet failures. Electric trains from 2030 remove those failures, which is how the plan adds a fifth more service and still holds the 90% floor.

points.lead: What the plan must not do
points.text: Adding off-peak trains before the depot extension opens would park units on running lines overnight and cost another point. The timetable change therefore waits for the twelve new sidings in December 2027.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; performance reports

pages.title: Dales and Valley gained off-peak journeys while the Coast line lost them
pages.bar: The two lines that gained most are the two with half-hourly stations, and the one that lost is hourly throughout: frequency, not the market, separates them.
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; ticket sales by line

pages.title: Punctuality has sat inside the target range for three years running

exhibit.heading: Trains arriving within five minutes, FY19-FY26

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

points.text: Punctuality sat under 90% in five of the eight years, with FY22's dip the result of a leaf-fall season run on an unchanged timetable.
Recovery time at the two busiest junctions lifted punctuality above 91% in FY24, and it has stayed in the range since.
FY26's 91.5% is a point and a half above the floor; one bad autumn would take the operator back under it.

pages.title: Journeys fell by a third during the six-week strike and recovered within a month
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

points.text: Journeys fell from 0.97 million a week in March to 0.61 million in May, the lowest week of the year.
By June journeys were within one per cent of March, and by September they were above it.
The six weeks cost about £9m in fares, of which delay-repay and season-ticket refunds were £2m, and none of it has been recovered from the dispute.

pages.title: Journeys reach 60 million by FY31 in four outcomes of five
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

points.text: The central forecast passes 60 million in FY31, and four outcomes in five land at or above the target.
Hybrid working and fares policy drive the spread; leisure growth alone keeps the low case above 50 million.
A fares settlement by FY28 would halve the width of the inner band by fixing the largest single input.

pages.title: Off-peak journeys on the trial lines grew 48% in three years, on hourly lines 9%

exhibit.heading: Off-peak journeys by group of lines

annotations.text: Half-hourly trial starts on the Dales and Valley lines
Coast units lent to the trial; its evening trains cut
Hourly lines flat at about 6 million since FY24

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: Northvale ranks sixth of eight operators on off-peak share of journeys

annotations.text: Half-hourly off-peak on every line since 2022
36%: still hourly on three of its five lines

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: Coast line stations wait twice as long off-peak as the Dales
pages.rail: The four stations with the longest waits are the four still served hourly. Their passengers wait 30 minutes on average for a train, against 15 at the half-hourly stations, and that wait is the reason drivers give most often for not taking the train.

exhibit.heading: Average off-peak wait for a train

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 timetable

pages.title: Every trial route gained off-peak journeys; Skipton gained most

points.text: The six routes that moved to a half-hourly off-peak service gained between 16% and 41% in two years, and Leeds to Skipton gained most because its hourly train had been the fullest. No trial route lost journeys, and the hourly routes beside them grew by 4% over the same period.

Surveys on the trial trains found that one journey in five had moved from the peak; the rest were trips not made by rail before. The trial ran on lines with spare units, so it says nothing about the Coast line, where the fleet is committed until 2030.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; timetable trial, FY24 to FY26

pages.title: Five of eight operating measures missed target in FY26, punctuality furthest

points.text: Five of the eight measures fell short, and punctuality and fleet availability, the two furthest from target, share one cause: the Eastern line diesel units, which fail three times as often as the rest of the fleet.
Cost per train-km and the customer score beat target, and revenue per journey meets it. The plan therefore starts from an operation that is short of trains that work, not short of money or goodwill.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 scorecard

pages.title: Northvale fills 47% of its off-peak seats, the fewest of the eight operators
pages.subtitle: Off-peak load factor, share of seats filled, FY26

annotations.text: Six-car trains run hourly where peers run two cars half-hourly
Westmoor halved train length in 2024 and doubled frequency

pages.source: Source: illustrative load data; synthetic

pages.title: The Airport line carries more journeys per km than the next four lines together
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

points.text: The Airport line carries 412 thousand journeys per route-km, more than the next four lines together, on just eleven kilometres of track.
The other seven lines run between 22 and 48 thousand, a spread the broken axis keeps legible.
Moving two of the newest units to the Airport line would add more seats where they are used than any other move in the fleet plan.

pages.title: The three biggest stations carry more than half of all journeys
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

points.text: Central, Harbour and Airport carry 22.8 million of the 40.9 million journeys, 56% of the whole.
The six suburban stations each carry less than the average of 4.5 million, and 44% between them.
Gate-line upgrades at the three core stations reach half of all passengers for a third of the budget, so they come first in the plan.

pages.title: The five methods value the Coast concession at £300m to £520m; our bid is £440m

exhibit.heading: Value of the Coast concession by method

points.text: The discounted cash flow puts the concession at £410m to £520m on the timetable recast, the method the board relies on most.
Trading multiples and the last four awards both bracket the bid, so it is neither the cheapest nor the dearest reading.
The asset base, at £300m to £360m, is what the fleet and depots fetch on their own, and sets the walk-away point.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

pages.title: Swiss and Japanese railways carry 47% and 44% of journeys off-peak, against Northvale's 36%

exhibit.heading: Share of rail journeys made off-peak, 2025

points.text: The four railways above 39% all run regional trains at least every half hour between the peaks, and none prices the off-peak more than 30% below the peak fare.
At 36% Northvale would rank sixth of the eight, between Denmark and Germany, on an hourly off-peak timetable on three of its five lines.
Reaching Austria's 42% on Northvale's 48 million journeys means about five million more off-peak journeys a year, with the peak left as it is.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic national benchmarks

pages.title: Commuting is half of City line journeys, a fifth of the Coast's
pages.bar: The lines with the most leisure travel are the ones with the fewest off-peak trains, so the timetable is thinnest where demand is most elastic.
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 passenger survey

pages.title: The City line is two fifths of journeys and the most peak-heavy

exhibit.heading: Journeys by line and time of travel, FY26

points.text: The City line carries 19.6 million of the 48.3 million journeys, and two thirds of them in the peak, where its trains are full. Growth there needs longer trains or more track, which the plan does not buy before FY31.

The Eastern and Coast lines together carry 3.2 million off-peak journeys on 11.5 million in total, the thinnest off-peak share on the network. Those two lines are where a half-hourly timetable has the most empty seats to fill.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; ticket sales by line and time of travel

pages.title: Forty-two of a hundred drivers name the wait, not the fare
pages.rail: The wait for the next train is named by 42 of the 100 drivers surveyed and the fare by 21. A timetable change addresses twice as many of them as a fare cut would, and it costs the operator less for each trip it wins.
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 survey of 100 drivers in the Dales corridor

pages.title: Three packages take four fifths of the capital programme

points.text: Overhead wires, the depot and fleet, and the power supply come to £520 million of the £640 million. Two of the three belong to electrification, which is why its dates decide when most of the money is spent.

Stations work of £45 million follows the housing sites and can slip a year without touching the timetable. The depot cannot: the half-hourly service needs its twelve sidings before the first added train runs in December 2027.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; capital plan, September 2026

pages.title: Over half of off-peak seats run empty across the network

points.text: Off-peak trains ran with 54% of their seat-km empty in FY26. The track, the crew and the fuel were paid for whether or not the seats were used, so a passenger in one of them costs nothing extra to carry.

points.lead: Why it is the first lever
points.text: Filling a tenth of those seats adds 1.9 million journeys with no new train. That is why the plan starts with the off-peak timetable and leaves the full peak for the electric fleet.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; seat-km from the FY26 timetable, loads from ticket sales

pages.title: Half of riders say trains do not run often enough; most say stations feel safe

exhibit.heading: Agreement with each statement, share of riders

question.text: How far do you agree or disagree with each of the following statements about your local rail service?

categories: Fares are fair for the journey

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

points.text: Half of riders disagree that trains run often enough, the only statement where disagreement outweighs agreement.
Fares split riders: 44% agree they are fair for the journey and 32% disagree, with a quarter undecided.
Six riders in ten agree that stations feel safe, and almost two-thirds that information is clear.

pages.title: Step-free access reaches 93% of City stations but only 41% of Dales stations

exhibit.heading: Stations with step-free access by line, FY26

points.text: Thirteen of the Dales line's twenty-two stations have stairs only, most of them single-platform halts built in the 1870s.
Ramps rather than lifts would serve nine of the thirteen at about £0.4m each, a third of the cost of a lift at a single-platform halt.
The Dales line carries the network's oldest passengers: one in four is over sixty-five, against one in seven across the network as a whole.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

pages.title: The largest hourly stations are where a half-hourly service pays most

exhibit.heading: Off-peak service, growth and size, FY23-FY26

points.text: Scarborough carries 1.9 million journeys a year on an hourly service and grew 6%, a third of the rate of stations its size with a train every half hour. Moving it and Selby to half-hourly reaches more passengers than moving Malton and Goole together.

points.lead: The threshold holds at every size
points.text: All six stations above 30 trains a day grew by 14% or more, whether they carry 0.9 million journeys or 3.4 million. Size changes how much a faster timetable is worth, not whether it works.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; ticket sales by origin station

pages.title: Empty seats cluster between the peaks on the Valley and City lines
pages.rail: The interpeak hours hold 61 thousand empty seats a weekday on the City and Valley lines alone, more than every other band on every other line together. The evening is emptier still on the Dales, where the last train leaves before walkers finish.
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; seats from the FY26 timetable, loads from ticket sales

pages.title: Each extra off-peak train an hour adds about eleven riders a train-hour

exhibit.heading: Off-peak frequency against riders, twelve routes, FY26

points.text: Across the twelve routes, each extra train an hour carries about eleven more riders a train-hour, with no sign of the line flattening at four.
Skipton runs one train an hour and carries 24 riders, close to the line: the route is held back by frequency, not demand.
A second off-peak train an hour on the Skipton line would add about £1.2m a year in fares at today's average yield.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic

pages.title: Only the Eastern line improved month after month once its timetable changed
pages.subtitle: Trains arriving within five minutes, eight lines, April 2025 to March 2026

exhibit.heading: Trains on time by line, FY26

points.text: The Eastern line rose from 80.3% to 91.8% over the year, gaining in eleven months of twelve, while the other seven lines ended within a point of where they began.
Eastern was the only line recast in April with slack at its two single-track sections; its fleet and its staffing did not change, so the gain is the timetable's.
Borders and Coast run the same single-track pattern and sit lowest at 83.4% and 84.9%; recasting their timetables is the cheapest punctuality gain the plan has.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; train running records

pages.title: Only the Eastern line moved its riders from season tickets to day tickets
pages.subtitle: Journeys by ticket type as a share of each line's journeys, six lines, FY24 to FY26

exhibit.heading: Journeys by ticket type and line

points.text: Season tickets fell from 47% to 28% of Eastern journeys; on the other five lines no ticket type moved over three points.
Eastern was the only line recast to a train every twenty minutes in FY25, and its fares did not change.
A day-ticket journey earns about a third more than a season journey, so the shift adds revenue; the Valley line is the next test.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic ticket sales

pages.title: Day tickets carry half the Eastern line's journeys and under two in five elsewhere
pages.subtitle: All eight lines, every journey in FY26 by the ticket its rider bought

exhibit.heading: Journeys by ticket type and line, FY26

points.text: Day tickets are 53% of Eastern journeys; on the other seven lines they run from 37% to 39%, and season tickets still lead on four of them.
The Eastern line is the one running a train every twenty minutes, and its riders now buy on the day; the timetable, not the fare, sets the mix the other lines will move towards.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; synthetic ticket sales

pages.title: Off-peak growth carried FY26, led by the most punctual lines
pages.rail: Off-peak journeys overtook the peak in the last quarter, and Dales and Valley - the two lines with half-hourly stations - led both revenue growth and punctuality.
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; ticket sales and train running records

pages.title: The City line earns 27% of revenue, more than half of it from season tickets

exhibits.heading: City line revenue by ticket, FY26

points.text: Season tickets earn £22m of the City line's £41m, a larger share than on any other line, because the line serves the two business parks at Thorpe and Holbeck.
Three office days a week have cut City season sales by a fifth since FY22, and the decline has not yet levelled off in the latest quarter's sales.
A carnet of eight returns at a season's daily rate would keep the commuters the season ticket is losing, at a cost of about £1.4m.

pages.source: Source: illustrative revenue data for a fictional operator; synthetic

pages.title: The plan cuts Northvale's cost per train-km by £2.10, level with Westmoor

exhibits.heading: Cost per train-km after the plan

points.text: Rostering to the recast timetable saves £1.20 a train-km, most of it in rest-day working on the Valley and Coast lines, where crews now cover gaps at overtime rates.
Regenerative braking on the Valley fleet saves £0.55 a train-km from 2028, once the two substations on the line are upgraded to take the returned power.
Closing the Malton depot and moving its overnight maintenance to York saves the last £0.35 a train-km, with no change to the fleet's availability.

pages.source: Source: illustrative cost data for four fictional operators; synthetic

pages.title: The Eastern line ran on time, emptier and richer once trains came every twenty minutes

points.text: Trains on time rose from 81.2% to 91.8% in the two years after the recast, because the slack at the two single-track sections absorbed the delays that used to cascade.
With a train every twenty minutes the peak spread out: trains over capacity fell from 27% to 9%, though the line carries more riders than before.
Fare revenue grew from £44m to £55m as riders moved to day tickets, which earn about a third more a journey than seasons.

pages.title: A timetable change needs four approvals, two of them in parallel

points.text: The path offer and the crew plan start from the same bid and run side by side for about fourteen weeks. Whichever finishes later sets the date of the safety case, and so far it has been the crew plan on every change.
A bid lodged after June 2027 misses the December 2027 timetable and waits for May 2028. Every other date in the Dales plan is set backwards from that bid.
The safety case cannot start until both branches report, so a late crew plan delays a path offer that was ready. Starting the crew plan four weeks before the bid removes that wait.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: The growth question splits into capacity and demand, and both say off-peak

exhibit.root: Can Northvale reach 60 million journeys a year by FY31, and where does the growth come from?

branches.label: Where is there capacity to carry more passengers?

conclusions.text: Not in the peak: trains run above 90% full on all five lines
Between the peaks: over half of off-peak seats run empty

branches.label: Where is there demand that the railway is not serving?

conclusions.text: Half-hourly stations grew off-peak journeys 16.5% in three years
Drivers name the wait for a train twice as often as the fare

exhibit.conclusion: Yes: fill the off-peak first with a half-hourly timetable, then electrify

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator
pages.bar: Both branches point the same way: the growth is between the peaks, where the seats are empty and a shorter wait is what passengers ask for, so the half-hourly off-peak timetable goes first.

pages.title: Four steps take the Dales line from hourly to half-hourly

items.label: Recruit crews
items.text: 36 drivers and guards in post by March 2027

items.label: Extend the depot
items.text: Twelve sidings open by November 2027

items.label: Win the paths
items.text: Timetable bid accepted in the June 2027 round

items.label: Run the service
items.text: Half-hourly off-peak from December 2027

points.text: Training a driver takes eleven months, longer than any other step, so recruitment started in 2026. Two of the three intakes are already in post and the third begins in January 2027.
The added trains need somewhere to stand overnight. Without the twelve new sidings, units would be stabled on running lines and the first morning trains would start late.
Paths are allocated twice a year. A bid accepted in June 2027 puts the service in the December timetable; one that misses it waits until May 2028 and costs 0.9 million journeys.

exhibit.foundation: Depot extension, 36 more crew and the 2029 power upgrade

pages.rail: None of the levers works without the foundation: the depot holds the added trains, the crews run them and the power upgrade feeds the wires. A slip there moves every date above it, so the board reviews it first.

pages.title: Four layers of cost sit under every train-km operated

layers.label: Variable: fuel and crew hours
layers.text: £6.10 per train-km; the only layer an added off-peak train incurs, and the one electric traction cuts by 40%

layers.label: Semi-fixed: fleet and maintenance
layers.text: £4.20 per train-km; set by how many units are owned, so it falls when the diesel fleet is retired

layers.label: Fixed: track access
layers.text: £4.10 per train-km; charged by the infrastructure manager whether or not the paths are used

layers.label: Fixed: stations and overheads
layers.text: £3.20 per train-km; staff, buildings and systems that every journey shares

points.text: An added off-peak train uses units and track already paid for, so it adds only the £6.10 variable layer, a third of the £17.60 average.
Electric trains' lower fuel and maintenance bills cut the Eastern line from £21.40 a train-km to £15.80, and the network average to £16.40.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: Four bodies share the timetable; the infrastructure manager sits between them

nodes.label: Northvale Rail
nodes.body: Bids for paths and runs trains

points.lead: Every path goes through one body
points.text: The infrastructure manager allocates paths to passenger and freight operators alike, so a half-hourly Dales service is a request to it, not a decision Northvale can take alone.
Six freight paths a day cross the Dales line between the peaks. Two have not been used since 2024, and the bid asks for those two rather than for new capacity.
The regulator approves access rights only for services the transport authority has agreed to fund, so the two approvals are sought in one submission in March 2027.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: Of 100 car trips in the corridor, eleven could move to rail

stages.label: Start and end near a station

points.text: Only 46 of 100 car trips start and end within a mile of a station; no timetable reaches the rest.

points.lead: The wait is the largest loss the plan controls
points.text: A half-hourly service takes the near-station trips facing a wait under 20 minutes from 14 to 27.
Price removes three trips where the wait removes fifteen, so the fare reform is sequenced last.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: Most new off-peak journeys come from the car, not from the peak

points.text: Of every 100 journeys the trial added, 48 replaced a car trip and 32 were trips nobody made before. Only 20 moved from the peak, so the trial grew the market rather than rearranging it.
Day returns took 58 of the 100, most of them bought by former drivers on the day of travel. That is the ticket a walk-up half-hourly service suits, and it earns the highest fare per journey.

points.lead: The peak shift is useful too
points.text: The 20 journeys that left the peak freed seats on the fullest trains and went mostly to flexible seasons, the product the 2030 fare reform extends to every line.

pages.title: The plan plays to two strengths and has to cover two exposures

quadrants.title: Strengths
points: Half the off-peak seats are empty
Dales units and crews are in place
Day tickets are already 47% of journeys

quadrants.title: Weaknesses
points: Eastern diesel fleet fails three times as often
No spare units on the Coast line

quadrants.title: Opportunities
points: Two unused freight paths on the Dales
Drivers name the wait, not the fare

points.text: The empty off-peak seats and the Dales crews are in hand today, so the first lever needs no new trains.
The Eastern fleet's failures and the Coast line's missing units share a cure: electric trains in 2030 free eleven diesel units.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: The timetable is the one lever that is both large and quick

points.lead: One lever in the top right
points.text: The off-peak timetable adds 5.1 million journeys and starts in December 2027, eighteen months before anything else of its size. No other lever is both large and quick.
It adds 3.8 million journeys but not before the second half of 2030, and it is the only lever that depends on someone else's work, the 2029 power upgrade.
Later last trains add 0.3 million journeys within a year for almost no capital. They ride on the timetable change and are bid for in the same round.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: Northvale sits nearer a commuter railway than the plan needs

points.text: Ticket sales have already moved most of the way to pay-as-you-go, with day and advance tickets now 74% of journeys. The timetable has not followed: it is still built around two peaks.

points.lead: Frequency is the gap to close
points.text: Three of five lines run hourly between the peaks. Moving them to half-hourly shifts the operator past the midpoint on frequency, the dimension passengers score lowest.
Only the City line is electric today. The Eastern line joins it in 2030, which takes electric running from a fifth of train-km to a half.

pages.title: Two lines are ready and worth growing; one is neither

points.text: The Dales and Valley lines have both the empty seats and the units, crews and paths to fill them. Their timetables change in December 2027 and May 2028.
The Eastern and Coast lines have the headroom but not the fleet. Electric trains in 2030 release the eleven diesel units that move them to the right.
The City line is ready but has the least headroom, since its off-peak trains are already the fullest. Its timetable is left as it is until FY31.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: Halifax and Huddersfield rose to the top on off-peak growth

points.text: Halifax ranked fifth on off-peak growth in FY23 and first by FY25, and Huddersfield rose from sixth to third. Both followed the Valley line's half-hourly timetable, introduced in May 2023, by one year.
Half-hourly since early 2023, Skipton led for two years and ranks second since. The three stations at the top are the three with a train every half hour between the peaks.

Scarborough and Hull, the ends of the Coast and Eastern lines, have ranked seventh and eighth in all four years, on hourly timetables that have not changed since FY23 and with no spare units to change them before 2030.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.title: One director answers for the recast; five leads each own a workstream

points.text: The programme director signs off the timetable, holds the £18m budget and reports to the board each month on cost, dates, risk and the passenger research.
Each lead owns a plan, a budget line and a risk log, and meets the director every week from now until the new timetable goes live in May next year.
A lead escalates any change over £250k or a week's delay; the director decides within five working days, and the board hears of each decision, with its cost, at its next meeting.

pages.title: Four of the five capabilities the passenger domain needs are missing

points.text: All four operational capabilities are in place and were rated mature in the FY26 capability review, two of them for the third year running.
Four of the five passenger capabilities are missing or run by hand, which is where the satisfaction scores fall furthest behind the peers.
The plan builds the journey planner and the seat map first, since both feed the customer-insight data that accessibility booking and insight itself need.

pages.title: Later weekend trains serve all three groups the plan targets

sets.label: Weekend walkers
sets.text: Want the hills and a late train home

points.text: A later last train on Saturdays and Sundays is the one change all three groups ask for, and it costs about £2.1m a year in crews and energy.
Group returns serve walkers and families alike; ramps at the halts serve older passengers and families with pushchairs.
What each group wants on its own - a hills timetable, lifts at the larger stations, family railcards - comes after the shared changes are in place.

pages.title: Five dates carry the plan; only the power upgrade is not ours

items.text: Thirty-six drivers and guards in post after three training intakes.

items.label: Timetable bid lodged
items.text: Asks for two unused freight paths, so needs no capacity study.

items.label: Dales service starts
items.text: Half-hourly off-peak trains from Leeds to Skipton, a later last train home.

items.label: Power upgrade delivered
items.text: The network operator energises the Eastern line's grid connection.

items.label: Electric trains run
items.text: Fourteen electric trains replace the Leeds to Hull diesels and free eleven units.

points.text: Each has a named owner; a slip costs one timetable round, which is six months.
A year's delay to the grid connection costs a third of the plan, so the bi-mode order is the fallback.

pages.title: Six stages take the plan from recruitment to 60 million journeys

items.label: Prepare
items.text: Train 36 crew, add twelve sidings and lodge the Dales bid.

items.label: Fill the Dales
items.text: Half-hourly off-peak service from December 2027.

items.label: Fill the Valley
items.text: Halifax and Huddersfield follow once their sidings are extended.

items.label: Electrify
items.text: Energise the Eastern line after the 2029 power upgrade.

items.label: Reform fares
items.text: Flexible season tickets and off-peak day returns.

items.label: Serve new homes
items.text: Four station housing sites, served by trains already running.

points.text: The first three stages need only crews, sidings and a bid, and pay back within 26 months, funding the fourth.

points.lead: The fourth stage is the bet
points.text: Electrification takes £390 million and waits on a power upgrade; placed fourth, a slip delays a third of the journeys.
Fare reform waits a year, so its products fit how people then travel.

pages.title: All four initiatives run at once in FY28, the year the timetable goes live

points.text: The timetable goes live, fares launch and station building starts in the same year, and all three draw on the same operations team.
Moving the fares launch to FY29 would free the commercial team for the timetable's first six months, at a cost of about £2m in deferred revenue.
The timetable date is fixed by the franchise; the station work is fixed by the grant's spending window.

points.text: The plan fills the 54% of off-peak seats that run empty, and it does so with the fleet it has: the half-hourly timetable uses units that stand idle between the peaks. Journeys rise to 60 million without the unit count changing before 2030.

Electric trains then replace the oldest diesel units on the Eastern line, which frees eleven for the Coast line and takes the cost of a train-km down to £16.40. Punctuality is held at its 90% floor throughout, because the added trains run when the track is free.

points.text: The wait is named by twice as many drivers as the fare, so a timetable change wins more of them than a fare cut, at less cost a trip.

points.lead: The demand is stated, not assumed
points.text: One in four drivers says a half-hourly train would get them out of the car weekly: 1.4 million journeys a year across the corridor.
Two thirds did not know the off-peak fare, so a cut would go unnoticed; the 2030 reform starts with simpler products, not lower prices.

items.label: journeys a year by FY31

items.text: £390m of it the Eastern line

items.label: of capital per added journey
items.text: Over the assets' 30-year life

items.text: From the first electric train

points.text: Half of the added journeys come from the off-peak timetable, which needs only crews, units already in the fleet and a depot extension, so the first five million arrive by FY28 whatever happens to the overhead line. The other half follow electrification and the new housing.

The payback rests on the power upgrade landing by 2029: a year's slip moves the first electric train, and the payback with it, by a year, but it leaves the timetable's journeys where they are, and the capital is drawn in tranches, so none of it is spent ahead of the milestone it pays for.

pages.title: The plan can win £96m of a £1.2bn leisure market

items.label: Regional leisure travel
items.text: Every leisure trip in the region, by any mode

items.label: Trips Northvale's lines serve
items.text: Trips between places the network reaches

items.label: What the plan can win
items.text: Trips moved to rail by the timetable and fares

points.text: Leisure travel in the region is worth £1.2bn a year, most of it by car, most of it at weekends and most of it to the hills and the coast.
Two-fifths of it runs between places the network serves, which is the market rail can compete for.
The timetable and fares changes can win £96m of that by FY30, a fifth of the market on the lines, if the later weekend trains run from next May.

pages.title: Four priorities decide every trade-off in the plan

items.title: Fill before build
items.text: Use the seats and paths that exist before buying new ones

items.title: Hold the 90% floor
items.text: No added train may cost the network its punctuality

items.title: Fund from fares
items.text: Each phase is paid for by the revenue of the one before

items.title: One owner per lever
items.text: Every milestone has a name against it from the first month

points.text: Fill before build puts the off-peak timetable ahead of electrification: it sells seats that already run empty, while the wires need £390 million before they carry a passenger. Holding the punctuality floor keeps the peak timetable as it is, since every train added there has cost a point.

When the depot extension and the station works competed for the FY27 budget, funding from fares decided it: the depot unlocks 5.1 million journeys within a year and the stations do not. The owner of each lever accepted the order because the rule was agreed before the budget was.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; programme board terms of reference

pages.title: Only a late power upgrade puts the 60 million target at risk

items.label: Power upgrade slips a year
items.text: Electric trains start in 2031, not 2030. Journeys reach 56.2 million in FY31 and 60 million a year later; the bi-mode order is placed as the fallback.

items.label: Timetable bid misses June 2027
items.text: The Dales service starts in May 2028 instead of December 2027. The plan loses 0.9 million journeys in FY28 and recovers them by FY30.

items.label: Housing sites are delayed
items.text: Two of four sites open after FY31. The plan loses 0.6 million journeys and £40 million of developer contributions, covered by contingency.

items.label: Off-peak demand beats the trial
items.text: Stations gain 20% rather than 16.5%. Journeys reach 62 million, and the Valley line needs longer trains two years early.

items.caption: Half-hourly on four of six lines

points.text: All eight are regional operators carrying 20 to 70 million journeys a year on mixed commuter and leisure routes, so differences in their off-peak share are not differences of scale or market. Northvale sits sixth of the eight on that share, at 36%.

Westmoor and Tideway moved to a half-hourly off-peak timetable in 2022 and now carry 48% and 46% of their journeys off-peak. Fenland is the peer for electrification: its unit costs fell 24% in the three years after its wires were energised.

pages.title: The Dales draw walkers who decide the day before they travel

pictures.credit: An illustration drawn for this example

points.text: Four in five Saturday passengers on the Dales line are on a leisure trip, mostly to walk. They choose the day by the forecast, so advance fares cannot win them.
A train every half hour out and a later one home: the last train leaves Skipton at 18:40, before most walks finish.
Saturday departures from Leeds between 09:00 and 11:00 run 88% to 97% full, while trains after 16:00 leave three quarters of their seats empty.

pages.title: Off-peak passengers choose the train by the wait, so the timetable comes before the fare

pictures.alt: Illustration of two passengers waiting on a platform as a regional train arrives

points.text: Lapsed leisure riders name the wait between trains twice as often as the fare when they say why they drove instead. An hourly train turns a missed connection into an hour on a bench, and a family that has waited once takes the car the next time.
points.highlight: twice as often as the fare

points.text: Two in three off-peak passengers travel with someone else, most of them in pairs or families. A fare that sells the second and third seat does more for them than a cheaper single ticket, which is priced for the commuter who already travels.

Passengers judge the service from where they stand: a departure board that says when the next train leaves, a shelter and a seat. Half the stations on the Dales and Valley lines have none of the three.
A train every half hour between the peaks, live departure boards at all forty stations and step-free access at the twelve busiest. The fare change follows in 2030, once the trains are there to sell.

pages.title: The journey planner sells the day out, not just the ticket

image.alt: The planner's destination page for a harbour day out
image.credit: An illustration drawn for this example

points.text: Each destination page opens on the place itself, with its walks, its cafés, the last train home and the fare for the day, before any timetable appears on the screen.
The fare shown is the off-peak return for the whole group, so passengers see the price of the whole day out before they pick a time to travel.
In the twelve-week pilot on the Dales line, three times as many visitors booked from a destination page as from the old timetable search, and they spent a fifth more.

pages.title: Leisure journeys added £31m; season tickets and repay took back £20m

points.text: More weekend and off-peak trips added £31m, the largest driver, and the trend has run for five years.
Season sales fell another £14m as office days held at three a week; the fall is slowing but not over.
The £18m regulated fares rise will not repeat at that size next year, and delay repay depends on punctuality holding above 90%.

pages.title: London and Manchester send three in five visitors from beyond the network
pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 ticket sales by origin station

points.lead: Three in five from two cities
points.text: London and Manchester send 1.46 million of the 2.45 million visitor journeys a year that start beyond the network, most of them bound for the Dales and the coast. Nearly all change at Leeds from an intercity train, so Leeds is the gateway: the connection there decides whether the trip continues by rail or by hire car.

Aligning the half-hourly Dales service with the London and Manchester arrivals cuts the average wait at Leeds from 31 minutes to 12. The demand model credits through tickets and timed connections with 0.8 million of the 5.1 million journeys the off-peak timetable adds, so the timetable is written around the intercity arrivals first.
